questions.question: Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that studies motion:
options: Including the forces that cause it
questions.explanation: Kinematics describes motion — position, velocity, acceleration, time — without regard to the forces that cause it. Dynamics, by contrast, deals with forces.

questions.question: Distance is best described as:
options: The straight-line gap between two points
The total length of path travelled
questions.explanation: Distance is the total length of path travelled. It is a scalar and is never less than the magnitude of displacement.

questions.question: Displacement is:
options: The change in position with direction
questions.explanation: Displacement is the change in position, including direction. It is a vector and its magnitude is never greater than the distance travelled.

questions.question: The magnitude of displacement is never greater than the:
questions.explanation: The straight-line displacement can never exceed the actual path length, so |displacement| ≤ distance travelled.

questions.question: If a body completes a round trip, its displacement is zero but its distance is:
questions.explanation: For a round trip, the start and end positions are the same, so displacement is zero while the distance travelled is non-zero.

questions.question: Speed is defined as:
options: Change in velocity per unit time
questions.explanation: Speed is the distance covered per unit time. It is a scalar quantity.

questions.question: Velocity is the rate of change of:
questions.explanation: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement with time: v = Δs/Δt. It is a vector.

questions.question: The SI unit of velocity is:
questions.explanation: Velocity is displacement per unit time, so its SI unit is m/s.

questions.question: Average speed is the total distance divided by the:
questions.explanation: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time taken.

questions.question: Uniform velocity means that:
options: Speed and direction both stay constant
questions.explanation: Uniform velocity means both speed and direction stay constant, so acceleration is zero.

questions.question: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity:
questions.explanation: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a particular instant, equal to the limit of Δs/Δt as Δt → 0.

questions.question: On a displacement–time graph, the instantaneous velocity is given by the:
questions.explanation: The slope of the tangent to a displacement–time graph gives the instantaneous velocity.

questions.question: A straight sloping line on a displacement–time graph indicates:
questions.explanation: A straight line on a displacement–time graph has constant slope, indicating constant velocity.

questions.question: A horizontal line on a displacement–time graph indicates that the body is:
questions.explanation: A horizontal line on a displacement–time graph means displacement is not changing, so the body is at rest.

questions.question: Acceleration is the rate of change of:
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time: a = Δv/Δt.

questions.question: The SI unit of acceleration is:
questions.explanation: Acceleration is velocity per unit time, so its SI unit is m/s².

questions.question: Uniform acceleration means that velocity changes by:
options: Equal amounts in equal time intervals
questions.explanation: Uniform acceleration means velocity changes by equal amounts in equal time intervals.

questions.question: Retardation is the term used when a body’s:
questions.explanation: Retardation (deceleration) is negative acceleration, used when a body’s speed is decreasing.

questions.question: A body moving with constant velocity has an acceleration that is:
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means no change in velocity, so acceleration is zero.

questions.question: A horizontal line on a velocity–time graph indicates:
questions.explanation: A horizontal velocity–time line means velocity is not changing, so the body has uniform velocity (zero acceleration).

questions.question: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives the:
questions.explanation: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives the acceleration.

questions.question: The area under a velocity–time graph gives the:
questions.explanation: The area under a velocity–time graph is ∫v dt, which gives the displacement.

questions.question: A straight sloping line on a velocity–time graph indicates:
questions.explanation: A straight sloping velocity–time line has constant slope, indicating uniform acceleration.

questions.question: A curved line on a velocity–time graph indicates:
questions.explanation: A curved velocity–time line has a changing slope, indicating non-uniform acceleration.

questions.question: The equations of motion apply to bodies moving with:
questions.explanation: The standard equations of motion apply only to bodies moving with constant acceleration.

questions.question: In the equations of motion, the symbol u stands for the:
questions.explanation: In the equations of motion, u represents the initial velocity.

questions.question: The velocity of body A relative to body B is found by:
options: Subtracting the velocity of B from that of A
questions.explanation: Relative velocity of A with respect to B is v_A − v_B, i.e., subtracting the velocity of B from that of A (vector subtraction).

questions.question: Which equation of motion does not involve time?
questions.explanation: The equation v² = u² + 2as does not contain the time variable t.

questions.question: Free fall is motion under the influence of:
questions.explanation: Free fall is motion under the influence of gravity alone, with air resistance neglected.

questions.question: Near Earth’s surface, the acceleration due to gravity is:
options: Dependent on the falling body’s mass
questions.explanation: Near Earth’s surface, g ≈ 9.8 m/s² and is approximately constant, independent of the falling body’s mass.

questions.question: Ignoring air resistance, a heavy and a light body dropped from the same height reach the ground:
questions.explanation: Ignoring air resistance, both fall with the same acceleration g, so they reach the ground at the same time.

questions.question: Who showed that all bodies fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass?
questions.explanation: Galileo showed that, ignoring air resistance, all bodies fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass.

questions.question: A body thrown vertically upward has a velocity at its maximum height that is:
questions.explanation: At maximum height, the vertical velocity of a body thrown upward is momentarily zero.

questions.question: At the highest point, the acceleration of a body thrown upward is:
options: Directed downward and equal to g
questions.explanation: Even at the highest point, acceleration due to gravity is g directed downward. Only the velocity is zero, not the acceleration.

questions.question: Ignoring air resistance, the time to rise to maximum height compared with the time to fall back to the launch level is:
questions.explanation: Ignoring air resistance, the motion is symmetric, so the time up equals the time down.

questions.question: After launch, a projectile moves under the influence of:
questions.explanation: After launch, the only force on a projectile (ignoring air resistance) is gravity, so it moves under gravity alone.

questions.question: The path of a projectile is a:
questions.explanation: The trajectory of a projectile under constant gravity is a parabola.

questions.question: The horizontal component of a projectile’s velocity:
questions.explanation: Ignoring air resistance, no horizontal force acts, so the horizontal velocity stays constant.

questions.question: The acceleration of a projectile throughout its flight is:
questions.explanation: Ignoring air resistance, a projectile’s acceleration is always g directed downward.

questions.question: Two projectiles launched with the same speed at complementary angles have:
questions.explanation: For the same launch speed, complementary angles (e.g., 30° and 60°) give the same range: R = v²sin2θ/g is symmetric about 45°. So ranges are equal.
